name: Bhimakali Temple
builtDisplay: 13th c.; new tower rebuilt in the 1920s
style: Kath-kuni timber-and-stone, blending Hindu and Buddhist forms
significance: Counted among the fifty-one Shakta pithas, this hill shrine at Sarahan was the tutelary temple of the rulers of the former Bushahr state. Its twin towers of interlocked timber and stone make it one of the best-known examples of Himachali kath-kuni building.
story: Devotees hold that the ear of Sati fell here when Shiva carried her dismembered body across the earth.

name: Hidimba Devi Temple
style: Tiered wooden pagoda with a 24 m shikhara over a cave shrine
significance: A wooden temple in the deodar forest of Dhungri, Manali, raised over the cave where the goddess is said to have meditated. It is the focus of the town's spring fair and of Navaratri worship, and is prized for its carved timber doorway and tiered roofs.
story: Hidimbi married the Pandava Bhima after he killed her brother Hidimb, and their son was the giant Ghatotkacha.

name: Manimahesh Lake
style: Small shikhara-style shrine at the lakeside
significance: A glacial lake at about 4,080 m below the Manimahesh Kailash peak, held sacred to Shiva and second only to Lake Manasarovar in regional esteem. Its annual Manimahesh Yatra draws large numbers of Gaddi and other Hindu pilgrims.
story: Shiva is said to have performed centuries of penance here, the lake forming from waters that sprang out of his matted hair.

name: Lakshana Devi Temple
style: Late Gupta wooden temple on a sandhara plan
significance: One of the oldest surviving wooden temples in India, commissioned by Meru Varman at his hill capital of Bharmour and still holding its 7th-century brass image of Durga. Its carved timber doorway and ceiling preserve early Shaiva and Vaishnava imagery rarely found intact elsewhere.

name: Jakhu Temple
significance: An old Hanuman shrine on Jakhu hill, at 2,455 m the highest point in Shimla. A 108-foot statue of Hanuman erected in 2010 has made it one of the city's most visited landmarks.

name: Baba Balak Nath Temple (Deotsidh)
style: Cave shrine on a hilltop
significance: The principal shrine of Baba Balak Nath, a folk deity widely venerated across Himachal Pradesh and Punjab, set in a hilltop cave at Deotsidh in Hamirpur district. Pilgrims come in largest numbers during the month of Chaitra.
story: The deity is said to have been born to a Gaur Brahmin family at Girnar Parbat before settling in the Himachal hills.

name: Renuka Lake Temple
significance: The largest lake in Himachal Pradesh and a Ramsar wetland since 2005, revered as the embodiment of the goddess Renuka, mother of Parashurama. A five-day fair each year around Prabodhini Ekadashi brings pilgrims from across northern India.
story: After the death of the sage Jamadagni, Renuka is said to have entered these waters and become the lake itself, promising her son Parashurama an annual reunion.

name: Trilokinath Temple
deity: Avalokiteshvara to Buddhists, Shiva as Trilokinath to Hindus
builtDisplay: 7th-8th c.; marble image dated to the 12th c.
dynasty: Early medieval Himalayan; columns attributed to King Lalitaditya
style: Curvilinear stone shikhara crowned by an amalaka
significance: A hilltop shrine above the Chenab in Lahaul, worshipped by Tibetan Buddhists as Avalokiteshvara and by Hindus as Shiva. Prayer wheels stand beside a lingam, making it one of the clearest surviving examples of Himalayan religious syncretism.
story: A raja of Kullu is said to have tried to carry off the marble image but found it immovable, and a sword mark on its right leg is pointed out as proof of the failed theft.

name: Tabo Monastery
style: Mud-brick Tibetan monastic complex of nine temples, stupas and chortens
significance: The oldest continuously functioning Buddhist monastery in India and the Himalayas, founded in 996 CE during the later spread of Buddhism in Tibet. Its murals and stucco images have earned it the name 'the Ajanta of the Himalayas'.

name: Key Monastery (Kye Gompa)
builtDisplay: present fort-monastery 17th c.; foundation traced to the 11th c.
dynasty: Gelug, era of the Fifth Dalai Lama
style: Tiered fort-monastery in the Chinese-influenced 14th-century monastic manner
significance: The largest monastery in the Spiti valley, perched at about 4,166 m above the Spiti river and home to some 250 monks. It is the valley's chief training centre for lamas and holds a notable collection of thangkas and murals.

name: Kheer Bhawani Temple
style: Marble shrine over a heptagonal sacred spring
significance: Built over a spring at Tulmulla, this is the most important temple of the Kashmiri Pandit community, who offer kheer to the goddess from which the shrine takes its name. Its Jyeshtha Ashtami mela is among the largest Hindu gatherings in Kashmir after the Amarnath yatra.
story: The goddess is said to have appeared in a dream to the Srinagar yogi Krishna Pandit Taploo and directed him to the buried holy spring.

name: Avantiswami Temple
style: Kashmiri stone temple architecture: central shrine in a colonnaded courtyard with corner shrines
significance: The ruined Vishnu temple raised by King Avantivarman at his new capital on the Jhelum, one of the finest surviving examples of 9th-century Kashmiri stone architecture. Its peristyle courtyard and carved plinths document Kashmir's Hindu building tradition before the 14th century.
story: Local tradition calls the ruins Pandav Lari, the house of the Pandavas.

name: Raghunath Temple
style: Brick shikharas with gold-plated spires and Sikh-influenced domes
significance: A complex of seven shrines in the heart of Jammu, begun by the first Dogra ruler Gulab Singh and finished by his son Ranbir Singh. Besides some three hundred carved images it holds a library of over six thousand Sanskrit manuscripts, including rare Sharada-script texts.

name: Alchi Monastery
dynasty: Rinchen Zangpo era; later Gelug under Likir
style: Tibetan architecture with strong Kashmiri influence; three-storeyed Sumtseg with elaborate wood carving
significance: A riverside temple complex holding some of the oldest surviving wall paintings in Ladakh, executed in a Kashmiri idiom that has vanished almost everywhere else. It is the best preserved of the foundations attributed to the translator Rinchen Zangpo.
story: Tradition holds that of twenty-one scholars sent by the Tibetan lama-king Yeshe-O, only Rinchen Zangpo and one other survived to bring Buddhism back to the western Himalaya.

name: Thikse Monastery
deity: Gelug school; a 15 m Maitreya Buddha in the main hall
style: Twelve-storey hilltop fort-monastery in the central Tibetan manner
significance: The largest monastery in central Ladakh, rising in tiers on a hill 19 km east of Leh and often likened to the Potala Palace in Lhasa. It houses a celebrated two-storey Maitreya image, a nunnery and a large collection of Buddhist art.
story: Two crows are said to have carried off the founder's ritual offerings and set them down in order at this hill, which he read as a sign to build here.

name: Lamayuru Monastery
builtDisplay: 10th-11th c.; oldest hall from the Rinchen Zangpo period
style: Cliffside gompa; the surviving Seng-ge-sgang temple is the oldest structure
significance: One of the largest and oldest monasteries in Ladakh, set above the eroded badlands on the Srinagar-Leh highway and home to about 150 monks. It preserves meditation caves, including one associated with the Indian scholar Naropa, and hosts well-known masked dance festivals.
story: Naropa is said to have dried up the lake that once filled this valley and founded the monastery on the bed it left behind.

name: Diskit Monastery
style: Tibetan hillside monastic architecture
significance: The oldest and largest monastery of the Nubra valley, founded in the 14th century and long the religious centre for its villages. Around a hundred monks live there and the gompa also runs a school for local Tibetan children.
story: A Mongol demon hostile to Buddhism is said to have been killed here yet kept returning, and his shrivelled head and hand are believed to lie inside one of the temples.

name: Spituk Monastery
deity: Gelug school (originally of the Red Hat order)
style: Terraced hilltop gompa
significance: A monastery on a hill about 8 km from Leh, founded in the 11th century and converted to the Gelug order in the 15th. Its name, meaning 'exemplary', recalls Rinchen Zangpo's prediction that an exemplary religious community would arise here; some hundred monks live there and a large Kali image is unveiled at the annual Gustor festival.
story: The arhat Nyimagung is said to have blessed the site before the monastery was founded.

name: Durgiana Temple
style: Gilded dome, marble causeway and silver doors, modelled on Harmandir Sahib
significance: Amritsar's principal Hindu temple, rebuilt in 1921 by Guru Harsai Mal Kapoor on a 16th-century site. It stands in the middle of a tank and deliberately echoes the plan and gilding of the nearby Golden Temple.

name: Devi Talab Mandir
builtDisplay: sacred tank said to be about 200 years old
style: Gilded sanctum with carved wooden doors beside an old tank
significance: A temple beside an old sacred tank in Jalandhar, counted among the fifty-one Shakta pithas and drawing thousands of pilgrims each year. Its precinct also holds shrines to Kali and a model of the Amarnath cave.
story: The site is said to mark where one of the parts of Sati's body fell when it was divided by the Sudarshana chakra.

name: Bhagwan Valmiki Tirath Sthal (Ram Tirath)
style: Modern complex with sacred pond, circumambulatory bridge, library and museum
significance: The Ram Tirath site west of Amritsar, rebuilt in 2016 as a large memorial complex around a gold-plated image of the sage Valmiki. It is the most important pilgrimage centre of the Valmiki community in Punjab.
story: Valmiki's ashram here is said to have sheltered Sita after her exile from Ayodhya, and to be where her twin sons Lava and Kusha were born.

name: Mata Mansa Devi Mandir
style: Painted shrine complex; the 1840 Patiala Shivalaya carries 38 wall-painting panels
significance: A complex of three shrines in the Shivalik foothills of Panchkula district, built by the ruler of Mani Majra in the early 19th century and extended by Patiala in 1840. Millions of pilgrims visit during the spring and autumn Navaratras.

name: Sthaneshwar Mahadev Temple
builtDisplay: present temple by Raghunath Rao Peshwa (18th c.)
dynasty: Maratha (Peshwa); site named by Pushpabhuti of the Vardhana line
significance: The Shiva temple that gives Thanesar its name, an ancient Kurukshetra pilgrimage site whose present structure was built by Raghunath Rao Peshwa. A gurdwara beside it marks a visit by the ninth Sikh Guru, Tegh Bahadur.
story: The Pandavas and Krishna are said to have worshipped Shiva here and received his blessing for victory in the Mahabharata war.

name: Jyotisar
deity: Krishna; the sacred banyan and an old Shiva temple
significance: The Kurukshetra site traditionally identified as the place where Krishna delivered the Bhagavad Gita, centred on an ancient banyan tree. It is a principal stop on the Krishna Circuit and has been developed with a museum and monumental bronzes.
story: Beneath this banyan Krishna is said to have counselled the wavering Arjuna and revealed to him his universal form.

name: Kalkaji Mandir
significance: A Kali temple in south Delhi opposite Nehru Place whose oldest fabric dates from the Maratha period and which gives the surrounding neighbourhood its name. It fills with pilgrims at the twice-yearly Navaratri fairs.
story: Legend holds that the goddess Kalika was born on the very spot where the temple stands.

name: Jhandewalan Temple
style: Octagonal Devi shrine on a stone platform with pavilion and circumambulatory path
significance: A major Devi temple in central Delhi founded by the cloth merchant Badri Das and run since 1944 by the Badri Bhagat Jhandewalan Temple Society. It is busiest during Navaratri and is known for large-scale community kitchens.
story: Badri Das is said to have dreamt repeatedly of a buried shrine on the hill, and on digging near a spring found an old image of Vaishno Devi in a cave, over which he raised the flag that gave the temple its name.

name: Laxminarayan Temple (Birla Mandir)
style: Nagara (north Indian) style adapted with modern construction, by Sris Chandra Chatterjee
significance: The first large Hindu temple built in Delhi, raised by the industrialists Baldeo Das and Jugal Kishore Birla and inaugurated by Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi's condition that it stay open to worshippers of all castes made it an early landmark of temple-entry reform.

name: Chhatarpur Temple (Shri Aadya Katyayani Shakti Peetham)
style: Vesara-style marble buildings with jaali screens, mixing south and north Indian elements
significance: Delhi's second-largest temple complex, founded in 1974 and spread over some 28 hectares with more than twenty shrines in three precincts. It draws its largest crowds during Navaratri.
story: Devotees tie threads to an old tree near the entrance in the belief that wishes made there are granted.

name: Yogmaya Temple
dynasty: Late Mughal era; rebuilding attributed to Hemu in earlier phases
style: Plain hall and sanctum with a truncated shikhara and dome inside a walled enclosure
significance: A small temple beside the Qutb complex in Mehrauli, held to be the only shrine of pre-sultanate origin in Delhi still in worship. It is the Hindu focus of the city's interfaith Phool Walon Ki Sair procession.
story: Yogmaya is said to have taken the place of the infant Krishna when Kansa tried to kill him, slipping from his grasp to foretell his death.

name: Hanuman Temple, Connaught Place
deity: Hanuman in his child form (Bala Hanuman)
builtDisplay: rebuilt 1724 (Jai Singh II); earlier shrine under Akbar
significance: A busy Hanuman shrine in the middle of Connaught Place, rebuilt by Jai Singh II of Amber in 1724 and claimed as one of five Delhi temples traced to Mahabharata times. Its spire is unusual in being crowned by a crescent moon rather than the customary Hindu finial.
story: Hanuman is said to have appeared to Bhima as an old monkey during the Pandavas' exile, humbling him when he could not lift the aged creature's tail.

name: Eklingji Temple
builtDisplay: present complex 15th-16th c. (Rana Kumbha, Rana Raimal); 8th-c. origin
significance: The tutelary temple of the Mewar rulers, first attributed to Bappa Rawal in the 8th century and rebuilt by Rana Kumbha and Rana Raimal after repeated destruction. The Maharanas ruled formally as the deity's regents, which made this complex the spiritual centre of the Mewar state.
story: The 15th-century Ekalinga Mahatmya credits the original shrine to Bappa Rawal, founder of the Mewar line.

name: Shrinathji Temple
builtDisplay: 1672 (Goswami Damodar Das Bairagi under Maharana Raj Singh)
style: Haveli-form temple modelled on the Nanda temple at Gokul, with a seven-flag kalasha
significance: The chief shrine of the Pushtimarg Vaishnava tradition, built in 1672 after the image of Shrinathji was carried from Govardhan to Mewar for safety from Aurangzeb. It is laid out as a household rather than a conventional temple, with kitchen, treasury and stable serving the deity.
story: Pushtimarg hagiography says Shrinathji came to Mewar to play chaupar with the princess Ajab Kunvari, who then begged him to stay rather than return to Braj.

name: Khatushyamji Temple
style: Rajasthani temple architecture in white Makrana marble
significance: One of Rajasthan's most visited shrines, in Sikar district, where the head of Barbarika is believed to be enshrined. Millions attend the Phalguna Mela, with its Nishaan Yatra procession of pilgrim banners.
story: Barbarika, grandson of Bhima, gave his head to Krishna before the Kurukshetra war and was blessed to be worshipped as Shyam in the Kali Yuga; a local ruler is said to have found the buried image after a dream.

name: Salasar Balaji
builtDisplay: mid-18th c. (268th foundation day marked in 2022)
significance: A Hanuman shrine at Salasar near Sujangarh in Churu district and one of the busiest pilgrimage centres of the Shekhawati region. Great fairs are held there in the months of Chaitra and Ashwin.
story: A farmer at Asota is said to have turned up an image of Hanuman while ploughing and offered it the bajra churma his wife had brought; that night both the local landlord and a devotee named Mohandas dreamt they should enshrine it at Salasar.

name: Mehandipur Balaji Temple
significance: A Hanuman temple in Dausa district known throughout India for its rituals of healing and exorcism, which draw pilgrims seeking relief from affliction believed to be caused by spirits.
story: Hanuman is said to have appeared here in his Balaji form thousands of years ago.

name: Ramdevra Temple
significance: A temple raised in 1931 over the samadhi of Baba Ramdevji, the Tanwar Rajput saint who founded the village. Its annual fair in the monsoon months draws devotees from several states without distinction of caste or creed.
story: Baba Ramdevji is said to have taken samadhi in 1459 at the age of thirty-three, having founded the settlement and dug the Ram Sarovar tank.

name: Galtaji
deity: Several shrines; the hilltop temple is dedicated to Surya
builtDisplay: from the early 15th c.; Sun Temple under Sawai Jai Singh II
dynasty: Ramanandi sampradaya under Amber and Jaipur patronage
style: Rajasthani and Mughal blend, with rounded pavilion roofs, carved pillars and frescoes
significance: A pilgrimage site in a ravine about 10 km east of Jaipur where temples are built around natural springs feeding a chain of sacred tanks. Long a leading centre of the Ramanandi Vaishnavas, it fills with bathers at Makar Sankranti.
story: The place takes its name from the sage Galav, said to have performed his penance here.

name: Govind Dev Ji Temple
deity: Radha and Krishna as Govind Dev Ji
style: Temple within the City Palace; its Satsang Hall spans 119 ft of unsupported concrete roof
significance: Jaipur's principal Krishna temple, set in the City Palace complex around images that Sawai Jai Singh II brought from Vrindavan. It is also where Baladeva Vidyabhushana composed the Govinda Bhashya, a foundational Gaudiya Vaishnava commentary.
story: The image is said to have been made by Bajranabh, Krishna's great-grandson, as one of three portraying his feet, chest and face.

name: Moti Dungri Ganesh Temple
dynasty: Kachhwaha of Jaipur, under Madho Singh I
style: Nagara-style temple below a hill palace with Scottish castle detailing, in limestone and marble
significance: A Ganesha temple below the Moti Dungri hill in Jaipur, built in 1761 and now visited by well over a hundred thousand devotees a year. It stands close to the city's Birla Mandir and is one of Jaipur's most popular shrines.
story: The sindoor-coloured image is held to be more than five hundred years old, brought from Gujarat to Udaipur and then carried to Jaipur in 1761.

name: Birla Mandir, Jaipur
style: Modern white marble temple
significance: A white marble temple in Jaipur's Tilak Nagar built by the B. M. Birla Foundation and opened in 1988. Its outer walls are unusual in carrying figures from other traditions, including Christ, the Buddha, Confucius and Socrates, alongside Hindu deities.
story: Tradition has it that a Maharaja sold the Birla family the land for the temple for a single rupee.
